{
  "need": "Identity",
  "secondary": { "name": "Competence", "showing_up": "The shutdown looks like avoidance, but underneath it is a real fear that he does not yet know whether he can build a life that means something." },
  "read": "He is almost 18 and the world keeps asking him to name who he is going to be, and he does not know yet. Every college conversation feels like a test he has not studied for, and shutting down is the only way to stop the clock. The status piece is real: being pushed to answer a question he cannot answer yet makes him feel small, like he is already behind.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "You stop bringing it up because the shutdown is painful to watch and you do not want to damage the relationship, but that silence lets the deadlines and the fear grow unchecked while he stays stuck." },
  "mentorMove": "Keep the conversation open but change what you are asking. Stop asking him to name a destination and start asking him to think out loud about what kind of life would feel worth living. You hold the expectation that he engages with the future; you let go of the expectation that he has the answers today.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The future is not optional to think about, even when it is uncomfortable.",
    "There are real deadlines coming and your job as his parent is to make sure they do not sneak up on him while he is avoiding."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "The format of the conversation can be a walk, a drive, a ten-minute check-in, whatever makes it easier to think out loud.",
    "The topic does not have to be college specifically; it can be interests, people he admires, things he would hate doing every day.",
    "He does not have to have a plan right now, just a willingness to explore."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I want to say something before I ask you anything. I know every time college comes up you go quiet, and I have been thinking about why. I do not think you are being difficult. I think it is a genuinely hard question and nobody has a clean answer at 17." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "Can I ask you something different this time, not about schools or majors? When you imagine yourself at like 25 or 30, what would have to be true for you to feel like your life is actually yours? Not what I want, not what looks good on paper. What would make you feel like it was worth it?" },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "I am not trying to pin you down. I just want to understand what matters to you so we can figure out together what makes sense as a next step. You know yourself better than any application or test score does, and I want to use that." },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "Here is what I need from you, and I am not backing off this part: I need you to stay in the conversation with me, even when it is uncomfortable. I have high standards for you, not because I want to pressure you but because I genuinely believe you are capable of building something real. What I am asking is not that you have it figured out. I am asking that you do not go silent on me." }
  ],
  "longGame": "The goal right now is not a college list. It is keeping the relationship open enough that he will actually tell you what he is afraid of, and that trust is what makes every concrete decision down the road go better. If he learns that bringing you his uncertainty does not end in a lecture, he will keep bringing you the hard stuff."
}
situation: My almost-18-year-old shuts down every time college or life after graduation comes up.
